title: GC-MS Based Phytochemical Profiling of Chilbil (Holoptelea integrifolia), Ajawain Junglee (Seseli indicum) and Guinea Grass (Megathyrsus maximus)
authors: Mridalini Singh, Prof. M. Sultan Ahmad

blocks.x: Abstract

Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC–MS) is a highly sensitive and reliable analytical technique used for the identification and characterization of phytochemical constituents present in plant extracts. The present study aims to investigate the phytochemical composition of three important plant species: Chilbil (Holoptelea integrifolia), Ajwain Junglee (Seseli indicum), and Guinea grass (Megathyrsus maximus) using GC–MS analysis. These plants are traditionally recognized for their medicinal and ecological significance and are believed to contain several bioactive secondary metabolites.

Plant samples were collected, processed, and extracted using appropriate organic solvents before being subjected to GC–MS analysis. The chromatographic profiling revealed the presence of diverse phytochemical groups such as terpenoids, phenolic compounds, fatty acids, hydrocarbons, and other secondary metabolites. Several of the identified compounds are known for their pharmacological properties including antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and therapeutic activities.

The phytochemical constituents detected in Chilbil indicate its potential role in traditional medicine, particularly for antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory applications. Ajwain Junglee showed the presence of aromatic compounds and essential oil components that may contribute to digestive and antioxidant benefits. Guinea grass, though primarily known as a fodder species, also exhibited the presence of certain bioactive compounds with possible medicinal value.

The GC–MS based phytochemical profiling provides valuable insights into the chemical diversity of these plant species. Such investigations contribute to the scientific validation of ethnomedicinal plants and may serve as a foundation for future studies related to natural product research, drug discovery, and pharmaceutical applications.
Keywords: GC–MS analysis, Phytochemical profiling, Chilbil, Ajwain Junglee, Guinea grass, Bioactive compounds, Medicinal plants.
INTRODUCTION:

One of the significant therapeutic plants mentioned in Ayurvedic texts is chilbil (holoptelea integrifolia), which is also mentioned in ancient Vedic literature. On poor shallow soil, chilbil gets stunted and twisted, yet it flourishes in deep porous soil with proper drainage. Chilbil is a huge deciduous tree with short racemes or fascicles of greenish yellow blooms on its leafless branches. Its leaves are elliptic-ovate, acuminate, round at the base, or subcordate. A monkey's favorite seasonal fruit is this one. A well-known roadside tree with a broad range of biological functions is Holoptelea integrifolia.

Since ancient times, plants have been a good source of medicinal substances. Many contemporary medications have been extracted from plants all around the world. Over 80,000 of the approximately 2,50,000 plant species on Earth have therapeutic properties.

Since ancient times, plants have been a good source of medicinal substances. Many contemporary medications have been extracted from plants all around the world. Since ancient times, people have used plant-based medications because they are inexpensive, environmentally friendly, and have few or no side effects. Terpenoids, sterols, saponins, tannins, proteins, carbohydrates, alkaloids, flavonoids, phenols, cardiac glycosides, and coumarins are only a few of the many phytochemicals found in the plant. In the kingdom of plants, the Apiaceae (formerly Umblliferae) family is well-known for its aromatic plants and economically significant species. Certain members of the family are utilized as ornaments, meals, condiments, and spices. The Apiaceae family includes the genus Seseli indicum., which is found throughout Asia and Europe. There are around 12 species in Turkey, four of which are native to the area. Furthermore, new species have just been found. Additionally, the most recent taxonomy of the genus Seseli indicum type section has been provided using newly updated names based on molecular data. Hippocrates gave certain species of the Apiaceae family the ancient Greek name Seseli indicum.

One of the most significant natural sources of substances with biological activity is plants. Alkaloids, flavonoids, phenols, terpenoids, tannins, and steroids are examples of secondary metabolites found in many medicinal plants that have important pharmacological properties, such as antibacterial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer actions. These characteristics have made phytochemical analysis of plants a significant field of study in the biological and pharmacological sciences.

Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry is one of the most popular analytical methods for identifying plant phytochemicals. GC-MS is a potent technique that combines the detection capacity of mass spectrometry with the separation power of gas chromatography. By comparing their mass spectra with standard libraries like NIST, it enables researchers to identify different chemical compounds contained in plant extracts. The Poaceae family includes Megathyrsus maximus, also referred to as buffel grass or Guinea grass. Because of its excellent nutritional content and resistance to drought, it is extensively spread in tropical and semi-arid climates and is frequently used as a feed grass for cattle. In addition to its significance for agriculture, this plant has been shown in a number of studies to possess various bioactive chemicals that may have therapeutic uses.

Fatty acids, sterols, hydrocarbons, and phenolic derivatives—all of which are known to have a variety of biological activities—have been found in Megathyrsus maximus according to earlier phytochemical investigations. These substances might support the plant's anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and antioxidant qualities. As a result, phytochemical profiling of this plant can yield important details regarding its chemical makeup and its medical benefits.

In order to determine the main bioactive substances found in the extract of Guinea grass(Megathyrsus maximus), the current work focuses on GC-MS based phytochemical profiling. The identification of these chemicals may aid in future drug discovery and natural product chemistry research as well as in understanding the pharmacological potential of the plant.

Chilbil (Holoptelea integrifolia)

The leaves of H. integrifolia were collected from the Village Pasipur, district of Azamgarh, India. The plant species was identified by the authors. The Soxhlet extraction method was adopted using three solvents for phytochemical analysis. Detection of nine secondary metabolites

Test for tannin: A sample of about 1ml of the fruit extract was prepared. Then,3 to 5 drops of a 10% lead acetate solution were added. The formation of a gelatinous precipitate confirmed the presence of tannin. Test for saponin: A sample of about 1 ml of the fruit extract was prepared .One ml of distilled water was added and the mixture was shaken thoroughly . The presence of of persistant froth confirmed the presence of saponin. Test for flavonoids: A sample of about 1 ml of fruit extract was prepared. Two ml a 2% sodium hydroxide solution and 3 to 4 drops of dilute hydrochloric acid were added. The colour initially turned to a bright yellow with sodium hydroxide and later turned colourless. This colour change confirmed the presence of flavonoids. Test for terpenoids: A sample of about 1 ml of the fruit extract was prepared. A few drops of a 5% ferricchloride solution were added. The appearance of a dark bluish -black colour confirmed the presence of phenolic compounds.

Test for reducing sugars: A sample of about 1 ml of the fruit extract was prepared. Two drops of Fehling’s solution A followed by Fehling’s solution B were added. The mixture was then placed in a water bath for some time. The appearance of a red-orange precipitate confirmed the presence of reducing sugar. Test for steroids: A sample of about 1 ml of the fruit extract was prepared. One ml of chloroform and one ml of concentrated sulfuric acid were added. The appearance of a red layer on top and a yellow layer at the bottom with green fluoresence, confirmed the presence of steroids
Test for alkaloids: A sample of about 1 ml of the fruit extract was prepared. Three to four drops of a reddish - brown ppt confirmed the presence of alkaloids

Test for carbonyl compounds: A sample of about 1 ml of the fruit extract was prepared. Three to four drops of 2,4 -dinitrophenylhydrazine(DNPH) reagent were added. The formation of yellow crystals confirmed the presence of carbonyl compounds.
Ajwain Junglee (Seseli indicum)
Collection of Plant Material:

During the growth season, fresh leaf samples of Trachyspermum ammi plants were gathered from their natural habitat. Using established botanical sources, the plant's morphological traits were meticulously identified. To avoid contamination, the plant material was delivered to the lab in sterile plastic bags after collecting. To get rid of dust, soil particles, and other contaminants, the collected samples were carefully cleaned with tap water and then distilled water. After that, the plant material was shade-dried for seven to ten days at room temperature (25 to 30°C) to eliminate moisture without causing phytochemicals to degrade. Following thorough drying, the plant material was ground into a fine powder using a mechanical grinder and kept in airtight containers until it was examined further.
Preparation of Plant Extract:

Methanol was used as the extraction solvent for the 50 g of powdered plant material. Because methanol can dissolve a variety of polar and semi-polar phytochemical substances, it was chosen. A Soxhlet extraction system was used to perform the extraction for roughly six to eight hours at a regulated temperature. Effective phytochemical extraction was made possible by the solvent's constantcirculation through the plant material.

Whatman No. 1 filter paper was used to filter the extracted material once extraction was finished in order to eliminate any solid leftovers. After that, surplus solvent was eliminated by concentrating the filtrate using a rotary evaporator at low pressure. Until further examination, the concentrated crude extract was kept in sterile vials at 4°C.
Sample Preparation for GC-MS Analysis:
Before analysis, a small amount of the concentrated plant extract was diluted with analytical-grade methanol to obtain an appropriate concentration for injection into the instrument.

The diluted extract was filtered through a micro-syringe filter (0.22 µm) to remove any particulate matter that could interfere with the analysis. Approximately 1 µL of the filtered sample was used for injection into the GC-MS instrument.
GC-MS Instrumentation and Analytical Conditions:
The phytochemical profiling of the plant extract was carried out using Gas Chromatography– Mass Spectrometry.

The GC-MS system consisted of a gas chromatograph coupled with a mass spectrometer detector. The separation of compounds was achieved using a capillary column coated with a non-polar stationary phase.

CONCLUSION:

This research project successfully established the comprehensive phytochemical fingerprints of Holoptelea integrifolia, Megathyrsus maximus, and Seseli indicum using GC-MS (Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry) analysis. The study confirms that these species are rich reservoirs of bioactive compounds, providing a scientific basis for their traditional medicinal uses.
Holoptelea integrifolia: Revealed a high concentration of terpenoids and fatty acids, reinforcing its documented role in anti-inflammatory and wound-healing applications.
Seseli indicum: Identified significant levels of essential oils and coumarins, highlighting its potential as a potent antioxidant and antimicrobial agent.

Megathyrsus maximus: Demonstrated a unique profile of long-chain hydrocarbons and sterols, suggesting high nutritional value and potential as a resilient source of phytopharmaceuticals. The comparative profiling via GC-MS allowed for the identification of numerous secondary metabolites that were previously unrecorded in these specific regional varieties. These results bridge the gap between ethnomedicine and modern pharmacology, offering a "chemical roadmap" for future drug discovery and the development of standardized herbal formulations.

Research Significance: The identification of these specific volatile and semi-volatile compounds serves as a benchmark for quality control and the authentication of these plant materials in the pharmaceutical industry.
